newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Burton spins off star Debenhams.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Burton spins off star Debenhams.

text.p: British retail group Burton Group Plc on Tuesday announced plans to spin off its highly profitable Debenhams department stores, and to reorganise its struggling fashion chains to try and boost growth.
The demerger will aim to capitalise on a revival in the fortunes of the department store, which has become one of the fastest growing retail sectors in the country.
Burton said the demerger would "significantly enhance" shareholder value and was in the best interests of the group's shareholders and customers.
News of the break-up boosted the retailer's shares, which stood 13 pence higher at 127.75.

Burton, the second biggest clothing retailer in Britain after Marks and Spencer Plc, said the remaining business, which includes Top Shop, Principles and Dorothy Perkins, would be reorganised into a single business, renamed, and would keep its existing listing.
"This proposal would result in two strong independent companies each with a strong cash flow, in which Burton Group shareholders would participate," the company said.
Chief executive John Hoerner, who will head the multiples business after the demerger, said the fashion chains had a long way to go before becoming a true growth business but had great potential.
"Multiples, quite frankly is a good business," he told Reuters in an interview. "But it has got a long way to go. So I would have to say that it is still a little bit of a recovery business."
But Hoerner said that he hoped to see a "real difference" in the performance of the fashion stores business when they begin trading under the new structure next spring.

Having been credited with masterminding Burton's dramatic turnaround from troubles in the British recession of the early 1990s, Hoerner said after working on Debenhams for 10 years it was a world class store.
Asked how long it would take to rev up the group's other businesses, Hoerner said: "I've been working on multiples for five years. I hope it isn't going to take another five."
Burton has successfully rebuilt gross profit margins and revamped its womenswear chains to boost profits.

But persistent problems with its Burton Menswear chain and investors' concerns that the recovery was running out of steam have dogged the shares in recent months. On Monday the shares had sunk to 112.5 pence, their lowest for a year.
The group's first half profits published in May were up 23 percent, but the sales performance from the multiples was not perky enough to reassure investors.
Debenhams, which has around 92 stores in Britain, made profits of 102.8 million pounds ($173 million) in the year to August 1996, a 21 percent increase on the previous 12 months.
The chain's sucess has contributed to a turnaround in the the fortunes of department stores, which have grabbed a significant slice of Britain's retail upturn over the past 12 months.
Rival retailer Sears Plc is already planning to demerge its Selfridges department store, and last year Harvey Nichols Plc was successfully floated by Hong Kong-based Dickson Concepts.
Debenham's sales jumped 10.4 percent in the 18 weeks to July 4, excluding home shopping, while the fashion multiples' sales were only 1.4 percent ahead, excluding mail order.

Debenhams as a newly-listed department store company will have Peter Jarvis, former chief executive of Whitbread, as its chairman while Terry Green will remain as its chief executive. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
